source.title: Scaling Laws or Threshold Effects: Exploring the Optimal Vocabulary Size for Balancing Performance and Efficiency in Low-Resource Languages
source.authors: Ao Han; Andong Chen; Yuan Sun; Xiao-Bing Zhao

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses parameter-and-data scaling laws as background but its experiments scale vocabulary size, not held-out cross-entropy against parameter count, training tokens, or compute, nor the compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own results for vocabulary expansion and downstream-task performance, but those results do not test any listed version's specified power-law, extrapolation, allocation, architecture-shape, modality/regime, or downstream model-scale claim. The vocabulary-scaling findings are recorded under fits_no_version. Its discussion of parameter/data scaling laws is background, not a tested result.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann scaling laws as motivation. Its experiments vary only the size of an added trilingual vocabulary during LoRA continual pre-training of fixed 1.5B–8B models. It reports downstream task scores, tokenization quality, training time and throughput. It never measures held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It fits no power law and searches no compute-optimal split. Its four model sizes are not a controlled model-scale sweep with downstream scores tied to scale or loss. No listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, but incomplete. The authors also report a 63,000-token Pareto knee point for BPE (Llama 2-7B). They report that the 79.5k BBPE configuration cuts continual pre-training time by over 71% across 1.5B–8B models. They conclude that joint scaling is constrained by model capacity, with large vocabularies hurting small models.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies joint trilingual vocabulary size, then uses LoRA-based continual pre-training and SFT and evaluates downstream quality and efficiency. It does not fit or test the original parameter-, token-, or compute-based held-out-loss scaling relations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported vocabulary-performance pattern depends on tokenization method (BPE versus BBPE), model size and iteration, vocabulary scale, and downstream task. Pareto choices also depend on the objective weights and robustness perturbations.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream performance as vocabulary is expanded depends on the tokenizer. Llama 2-7B (BPE) rises roughly monotonically, saturating near 27k joint tokens. Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen2.5-1.5B (BBPE) dip below the no-expansion baseline under about 9k tokens, then gain. Qwen2.5-1.5B collapses above 150k tokens, which the authors attribute to the embedding-parameter share.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In low-resource vocabulary expansion, downstream gains from added vocabulary are monotonic for BPE but threshold-shaped for BBPE. Large-vocabulary penalties appear in small models.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2026
record.problems: The study does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fit the scaling relations in the claim. Its experiments cover 1.5B–8B models and a joint trilingual setting; some performance trajectories are presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Left out task-by-task and language-by-language vocabulary-sweep values, tokenization-quality measures, efficiency and throughput results, Pareto rankings, and JTE-versus-IME comparisons (Sections 4.2–5 and Appendices B–C): these do not measure any listed claim version. The retained rows summarize the text-described downstream vocabulary-scale patterns.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss swept over parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs used to extrapolate to larger runs.
No depth, width or shape comparison at fixed parameter count. Embedding growth from vocabulary changes the parameter count itself.
The fine-tuning/adaptation regime is present, but no power law in parameters, data or compute is fitted there.
Downstream scores are reported against vocabulary size, not against model scale or pretraining loss. The 1.5B vs 7B comparison only concerns where the vocabulary threshold falls.
No fitted parameter, data or compute exponents are compared across fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The title asks 'Scaling Laws or Threshold Effects', but 'scaling' here refers to vocabulary size, not to the parameter/data/compute laws of the originals. The L5 level comes from the Tao et al. (2024) vocabulary scaling law, not from the original sources. I agree with the reader's classification: discusses / T6.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fits from smaller runs or comparison of their predictions with larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of whether the claimed power-law form generalizes to other modalities or training regimes; the study varies vocabulary during low-resource text-model adaptation.
Downstream task scores are measured across vocabulary sizes, not model scale or pretraining loss as specified by this version.
No fitted parameter/data/compute exponents or compute-optimal split are compared across fitting choices.

rows.subject: Llama 2-7B
rows.operation_detail: Swept joint trilingual vocabulary expansion levels and evaluated downstream tasks.

conditions.value: machine translation, text summarization, text classification
140 to 195,000 tokens; trend described through approximately 27,000 tokens

rows.value: Overall upward trend with small early-stage fluctuations; performance rises steadily until saturating at approximately 27,000 joint tokens, then has diminishing marginal utility.
rows.uncertainty: Welch’s t-tests for initial small-scale variations: p > 0.05.
rows.note: This is vocabulary-scale performance, not held-out pretraining loss or performance across model scale.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Swept joint trilingual vocabulary expansion levels and evaluated downstream tasks.

conditions.value: machine translation, text summarization, text classification

rows.value: Performance degrades below the 9,000-token threshold, recovers to baseline around the threshold, and shows non-linear gains after crossing it; gains later diminish.
rows.uncertainty: For machine translation, p < 0.05 for the initial dip and subsequent recovery.
rows.note: The paper characterizes this as a vocabulary-dependent threshold pattern, not a test of parameter/token/compute power laws.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Replicated the joint trilingual vocabulary sweep and evaluated downstream tasks.

conditions.value: machine translation, text summarization, text classification

rows.value: The decline-then-rise trajectory is reported, with the inflection point at 9,000 tokens; the paper states that 79,500 tokens captures over 92% of maximum downstream-task gains for this model, while 195,000 tokens reaches its theoretical performance peak.
rows.note: The downstream results are across vocabulary configurations, not model-scale extrapolation.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-1.5B
rows.operation_detail: Replicated the joint trilingual vocabulary sweep and evaluated downstream tasks.

conditions.value: machine translation, text summarization, text classification

rows.value: The decline-then-rise trajectory is reported around the 9,000-token threshold; performance collapses at ultra-large vocabulary scales above 150,000 tokens.
rows.note: The reported collapse concerns vocabulary expansion in this small model, not departure from a fitted parameter/token/compute power law.
rows.check: The 'reversed' state has no version to be reversed against. Measured against the row's own described effect (a collapse above 150k tokens in Qwen2.5-1.5B, stated in Appendix B.1), the effect is observed. It would be reversed only relative to the monotonic-gain pattern of the other models, which is not a claim version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
